title: Burns: initial assessment and fluid resuscitation
subject: surgery-trauma
summary: Stop the burning and cool with running water, secure the airway early if inhalation injury is suspected, estimate TBSA (rule of nines, Lund and Browder in children), start formal fluid resuscitation at 2 to 4 mL/kg/%TBSA titrated hourly to urine output, and refer early to a burns unit.

sections.title: First aid
items: Stop the burning process: remove the patient from the source, remove burnt clothing and jewellery, and brush off dry chemicals before irrigating.
Cool the burn with cool (not ice-cold) running tap water for 20 minutes; it still helps if started up to 3 hours after injury. Do not apply ice.
Keep the patient warm while cooling the wound; avoid prolonged cooling of large burns, especially in children and older adults, because of hypothermia.
Chemical burns: irrigate with large volumes of water for a prolonged period (eyes until pH is normal); identify the agent.
Do not apply paste, oil, ghee, haldi (turmeric), toothpaste or raw cotton. Cover with cling film laid in strips (not wrapped round a limb) or a clean sheet for transfer.

sections.title: Primary survey and burn assessment
items: Assess as a trauma patient (ABCDE): look for associated injuries from blasts, falls or road traffic crashes, and for carbon monoxide or cyanide poisoning.
Inhalation injury clues: enclosed-space fire, facial burns, singed nasal hair, soot in the mouth or sputum, hoarseness, stridor, cough, respiratory distress.

Depth: superficial (red, painful, no blisters) is not counted in TBSA; superficial partial thickness (blisters, moist, blanching, painful); deep partial thickness (blotchy, sluggish capillary refill, reduced pain); full thickness (white, leathery or charred, painless).
TBSA in adults by rule of nines: head 9%, each arm 9%, front of trunk 18%, back of trunk 18%, each leg 18%, perineum 1%. The patient's palm with fingers is about 1% for scattered burns.
Children: use a Lund and Browder chart, because the head is proportionally larger and the legs smaller than in adults.
In India, flame burns in young women and burns in children may be medico-legal or non-accidental: document carefully, register as a medico-legal case per local law, and screen for abuse.

sections.title: Airway and breathing
items: Give high-flow oxygen by non-rebreather mask to all significant burns and smoke exposures; SpO2 is falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning, so measure carboxyhaemoglobin on a blood gas.

Intubate early with an uncut tube by the most experienced operator if there is stridor, hoarseness with progressive swelling, deep facial or circumferential neck burns, or a falling GCS; airway oedema worsens over the first 24 to 48 hours.
Suspected cyanide toxicity (enclosed-space fire with shock, coma or lactate that does not clear): hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV over 15 minutes.
Circumferential full-thickness chest or abdominal burns restricting ventilation need urgent escharotomy.

sections.title: Fluid resuscitation
items: Formal IV resuscitation for burns of 20% TBSA or more in adults and 10% or more in children, via 2 large-bore cannulae (through burnt skin if necessary) or intraosseous access.

Adults: start Ringer lactate at 2 mL/kg/%TBSA over 24 hours (ABA 2024 guideline, the modified Brooke volume); the Parkland formula uses 4 mL/kg/%TBSA. Give half in the first 8 hours from the time of burn (not arrival) and half over the next 16 hours.
Children: 3 mL/kg/%TBSA Ringer lactate by the same schedule, plus dextrose-containing maintenance fluid in children under 30 kg (ABA ABLS teaching); check glucose regularly.
The formula only sets the starting rate: adjust hourly to urine output of 0.5 mL/kg/h (about 30 to 50 mL/h) in adults and 1 mL/kg/h in children under 30 kg. Avoid over-resuscitation (fluid creep).
Consider albumin within the first 24 hours when volumes are running high (ABA 2024). Avoid hydroxyethyl starch.
High-voltage electrical injury: start at 4 mL/kg/%TBSA and target urine output 75 to 100 mL/h until pigmented urine clears; cardiac monitoring and CK.

sections.title: Wound, limb and supportive care
items: Escharotomy for circumferential deep burns of a limb with vascular compromise or of the torso with restricted ventilation; do not wait for pulses to disappear. Elevate burnt limbs.
Give titrated IV opioid analgesia; oral or IM routes are unreliable in major burns.
Tetanus prophylaxis according to immunisation status. Do not give systemic prophylactic antibiotics.
Insert a urinary catheter for burns needing formal resuscitation; nasogastric tube for major burns and early enteral feeding.
Clean and dress the wound with a non-adherent or antimicrobial dressing only after discussion with the burns unit; do not delay transfer for dressings.

sections.title: Monitoring
items: Hourly urine output, heart rate, blood pressure, temperature and fluid balance; lactate and base deficit on blood gas.
Watch for abdominal compartment syndrome (rising bladder pressure, tense abdomen, rising airway pressures) and raised intraocular pressure in large resuscitations.
Re-check distal perfusion of circumferentially burnt limbs hourly; monitor glucose in children.

sections.title: Refer to a burns unit (ABA criteria)
items: Immediate consultation with consideration of transfer: any full-thickness burn, partial-thickness burns of 10% TBSA or more, and deep burns of the face, hands, feet, genitalia, perineum or over major joints.
All suspected inhalation injuries, all chemical injuries, high-voltage (1000 V or more) electrical injuries and lightning.
Burns with significant comorbidity or associated trauma, and children (14 years or younger or under 30 kg), who may benefit from burns unit care.
Smaller partial-thickness burns, low-voltage electrical injury and possible smoke inhalation without clear signs: discuss with the burns unit.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Overestimating TBSA by including simple erythema, or underestimating it in children by using the adult rule of nines.
Following the formula rigidly instead of titrating to urine output; both under- and over-resuscitation cause harm.
Timing the formula from arrival rather than from the burn.
Delaying intubation until airway swelling makes it impossible.
Missing carbon monoxide poisoning because SpO2 looks normal.

drugs.name: Ringer lactate (adults)
drugs.dose: Start 2 mL/kg/%TBSA over 24 hours (Parkland: 4 mL/kg/%TBSA); half in first 8 hours from burn, half over next 16 hours
drugs.notes: Titrate hourly to urine output 0.5 mL/kg/h (30 to 50 mL/h).

drugs.name: Ringer lactate (children)
drugs.dose: 3 mL/kg/%TBSA over 24 hours, same 8 and 16 hour split, plus dextrose-containing maintenance fluid if under 30 kg
drugs.notes: Target urine output 1 mL/kg/h in children under 30 kg.

drugs.name: Ringer lactate (high-voltage electrical injury)
drugs.notes: Target urine output 75 to 100 mL/h until pigmented urine clears.

drugs.name: Oxygen
drugs.notes: Continue until carbon monoxide poisoning is excluded or treated.

drugs.name: Hydroxocobalamin
drugs.dose: Adults 5 g IV over 15 minutes; children 70 mg/kg IV (maximum 5 g)
drugs.notes: Suspected cyanide poisoning after enclosed-space fire.

sources.title: American Burn Association Clinical Practice Guidelines on Burn Shock Resuscitation
